title: The gari class: things whose plural is marked by ma-
goal: Shop for fruit and vegetables, say quantities and prices, and set up the noun class that holds almost every fruit name — the class whose plural begins with *ma-*.
bekal: its subject prefixes: *li-* for one, *ya-* for many
adjectives of this class: *kubwa → makubwa*, *-eupe → jeupe / meupe*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Matunda ya asubuhi
dialogs.intro: Early morning at the fruit market. Amina teaches Budi to name what goes in the shopping basket.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Today we're buying fruit and vegetables.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ninataka maembe. Embe moja ni bei gani?
lines.id: I'd like some mangoes. How much is one mango?
lines.literal: I-am-wanting mangoes. mango one is price which?

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.text: Embe moja ni mia tano. Maembe matano ni elfu mbili.
lines.id: One mango is five hundred. Five mangoes are two thousand.
lines.literal: mango one is hundred five. mangoes five is thousand two.

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.text: Mabivu kabisa! Yanatoka shambani leo asubuhi.
lines.id: Perfectly ripe! They came from the farm this morning.
lines.literal: ripe-ones completely! they-are-coming-from at-farm today morning.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Tunahitaji machungwa pia, na mayai kumi.
lines.id: We need oranges too, and ten eggs.
lines.literal: we-are-needing oranges also, and eggs ten.

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.text: Mayai yako hapa, ndani ya sanduku dogo.
lines.id: Your eggs are here, in a small box.
lines.literal: eggs they-are-located here, inside of box small.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Na hili ni nini? Jina lake ni nini?
lines.id: And what's this? What's it called?
lines.literal: and this-thing is what? name of-it is what?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Hili ni tunda la hapa. Jina lake ni fenesi.
lines.id: That's a local fruit. It's called fenesi.
lines.literal: this-thing is fruit of here. name of-it is jackfruit.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Fenesi? Kwetu tunaita nangka! Tunda hili ni kubwa sana.
lines.id: Fenesi? Back home we call it nangka! This fruit is huge.
lines.literal: jackfruit? at-our-place we-are-calling nangka! fruit this is big very.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Ni tamu pia. Duka lile linauza maji ya matunda.
lines.id: It's sweet too. That shop sells fruit juice.
lines.literal: is sweet also. shop that it-is-selling water of fruits.

lines.text: Vizuri! Sasa mifuko yetu ni mizito kabisa.
lines.id: Great! Now our bags are really heavy.

notes: **Fenesi is jackfruit, and it's not the only surprise in the Zanzibar market.** The East African coast has a tropical climate, so the basket looks tropical too: *nanasi* (pineapple), *embe* (mango), *nazi* (coconut), *mchicha* (spinach), *muhogo* (cassava), *ndizi* (banana), *papai* (papaya), *pilipili* (chili), *tangawizi* (ginger), *mdalasini* (cinnamon). Zanzibar is even nicknamed the Spice Island, for the same reason as Indonesia's Maluku.

**Shambani means "on the farm", from shamba (field; farm).** It is one of the first words to recognize once you leave town: most fruit in the market is described as *ya shambani* — from the farm, not from a warehouse. Remember the *-ni* ending from unit 8; it works here exactly the same way.
**Kuita means "to call; to name".** *Tunaita nangka* = we call it nangka. *Unaitwaje?* (what are you called?) is another way to ask a name, and the answer is *Ninaitwa Budi*.

**Kwetu means "at our place" — and holds a whole home town inside it.** *Kwetu*, *kwenu*, *kwao* are used for home, village or country of origin. When a Tanzanian says *kwetu*, it can mean "at our house" or "in our country", and context chooses.

**Mia tano means five hundred, not one hundred five.** Hundreds are built the reverse of the English habit: *mia* (hundred) first, then the multiplier. *Mia mbili* = two hundred, *mia sita* = six hundred.

grammars.title: The JI-/MA- class: none for one, ma- for many
body: This class holds fruits, paired things, big things and a large number of loanwords. The singular is often **without any prefix**, and the plural is marked by **ma-**.
after: The singular **takes no prefix on adjectives** — *gari kubwa*, *duka dogo* — except before an adjective that starts with a vowel, which takes *j-*: *yai jeupe* (white egg), *jicho jekundu* (red eye), *gazeti jipya* (new newspaper).

The plural uses **ma-** everywhere: *magari makubwa*, *matunda matamu*, *majina mazuri*. Before a vowel, *ma-* merges: *ma + eupe* → **meupe**, *ma + eusi* → **meusi**, *ma + ekundu* → **mekundu**, *ma + pya* → **mapya**.

Some words in this class **exist only in the plural** and never in the singular: *maji* (water), *maziwa* (milk), *mafuta* (oil), *maisha* (life). If you meet a word starting with *ma-* that makes no sense as a plural, it is probably one of this group.

grammars.title: Li- and ya-: the subject prefixes of this class
body: Just as the *nyumba* class uses *i-* and *zi-*, the *gari* class uses **li-** for one and **ya-** for many. Possessives and connectors: **langu / yangu** and **la / ya**.

head: Sentence
Meaning
Its negative
rows: The mangoes come from the farm.

after: Now you can reread sentences you've been using since unit 1: *jina langu*, *jina lako*, *jina lake* use *l-* precisely because *jina* belongs to this class. So does *soko liko mbele ya benki* in unit 8.

The demonstratives: *hili* / *haya* (this), *hilo* / *hayo* (that, just mentioned), *lile* / *yale* (that over there). Notice *haya* — the same word as the "okay" you used in unit 5, and the origin really is the same: "these things".

With this you hold **four of the six classes**: people (*mtu*), made things (*kitabu*), the biggest class (*nyumba*), and this one (*gari*). The two remaining — the *mti* class and the *u-* class — wait in unit 16.

sections.title: Matunda na mboga — what goes in the basket

blocks.text: *Tikitimaji* literally means "water pumpkin", and *maji ya nazi* is coconut water. Notice that many fruit names belong to the *nyumba* class (singular = plural): *ndizi*, *nazi*, *nyanya*, *pilipili*. Those in the *ma-* class are usually big fruits counted one by one.

Market quantities in East Africa are often given as *fungu* (a bunch; a pile) and *lundo* (a heap): *fungu la nyanya* (a pile of tomatoes). If you want to buy just a little, the sentence is *Nataka kidogo tu*.

blocks.text: Sentences to bring to the table: *Chakula hiki ni kitamu sana* (this food is delicious), *Nimeshiba* (I'm full), and *Sili nyama* (I don't eat meat) for vegetarians. For halal meat, *nyama ya halali* is understood all along the coast — most of Zanzibar and the Tanzanian coast is Muslim.

Ugali is eaten with the right hand: a small ball is rolled, pressed with the thumb into a hollow, then used to scoop up the sauce. It's a way of eating that feels natural at once — and your host will smile to see that a guest needs no teaching.
